articles.title: 'The polls are biased. The right always gets stronger': Likud’s quiet winner is suddenly hard to ignore
articles.body:
While much of the discussion surrounding last week's Likud primaries focused on reserved slots, political hit lists, recommended-candidate slates and speculation about party heavyweights Amir Ohana, Tally Gotliv, Yariv Levin and Shlomo Karhi, Energy Minister Eli Cohen preferred to run a campaign under the radar. It paid off.
Cohen finished first by a huge margin over the second- and third-place candidates, after also finishing near the top in the previous Likud primary. Likud members clearly like him, but to most Israelis he remains something of an enigma, with relatively little known about him. That is his weakness — and his strength.
“I’m certainly happy with the result,” Cohen said in his first interview since his primary victory. “Likud members are smart people who love the country. They chose a strong slate of people who get things done. And I want to tell you that in every ministry I’ve served in, I’ve proven myself through actions and delivered results for the public. The word ‘give up’ doesn’t exist for me.”
How does your victory square with the populist, combative rhetoric within Likud?
“Today, people want to choose someone who gets things done, not someone who only talks. And thank God, succeeding time after time speaks for itself. During the primaries, I didn’t campaign against anyone. I focused mainly on what I had done: how I managed to break the Israel Electric Corp.’s monopoly, how I ensured that the energy sector functioned flawlessly, how I reached a gas deal with Egypt and how I secured visa-free travel to the United States.”
So you cracked the formula for beating populism and shouting.
“Yes. I think actions beat populism and shouting.”
Before the primaries, no one was talking about Eli Cohen. Did that help you take the top spot?
“In the previous primaries, they predicted I would finish sixth, and I finished second. This time, they thought I would finish in the top three — and I came first. I had a feeling that this time, too, I would beat the polls. But I know one thing: I get up every morning at 7 and work all day for the good of the country.”
Finishing first in the Likud primaries is indeed an impressive political achievement and a statement of intent about the future. Moshe Kahlon, Gideon Sa’ar, Gilad Erdan and Yuli Edelstein have all been there before.
“I’m glad that, like them, I managed to finish first.”
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also politically destroyed all four of them.
“I will continue working with Netanyahu, and I’m pleased to have his confidence. Netanyahu is the right person to lead the State of Israel for the next four years. I think he delivered unprecedented achievements during this term. From the devastation of Oct. 7, we have become the strongest power in the Middle East.”
Do you see yourself running for the Likud leadership after Netanyahu?
“That question isn’t relevant right now. We are two and a half months out from an election, and I’m focused on one thing only: ensuring that Likud, led by Netanyahu, wins.”
Why are Likud ministers afraid to say that they are worthy and capable of replacing Netanyahu one day? Are you so afraid of him that you can’t bring yourselves to say it?
“We are on the eve of an election, and what is special about Likud is that we are united around Netanyahu. Likud is the most democratic party, compared with the left, which is constantly working to eliminate its own leaders. You can see they have nothing except ‘Anyone but Bibi.’”
Why did Netanyahu demand nine reserved spots on the slate? Doesn’t he trust Likud members?
“I think the prime minister looks at other parties, where the party leader determines the entire slate however he sees fit, and that is why he wanted those reserved spots for himself as well. In the end, the prime minister determines 25% of the slate through reserved slots, while 75% is determined by party members.”
Not simply a treasurer
Cohen, 53, began the current government’s term as foreign minister before moving to the Energy Ministry as part of an internal political arrangement. He has his sights set high. The next job he is eyeing is finance minister.
“I definitely expect to hold a senior position in the next government,” he said. “The three most senior portfolios are foreign affairs, finance and defense. Since I’ve already been foreign minister, the Finance Ministry interests me. I think that in the next term, the Finance Ministry must remain in Likud’s hands, and I have the qualifications for the job: my experience in the business world, my training as an accountant and my personal background. I would want to lead a free-market economy with social sensitivity.”
What do you think of Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich?
“In my view, the finance minister should not be the treasurer who simply hands out money. A finance minister needs to grow the pie, create engines of growth, ensure that young people want to live in this country, give them the opportunity to earn a decent living and work to reduce social disparities.”
Is it a mistake to appoint a finance minister who represents a particular sector?
“As I said, the Finance Ministry must remain with the ruling party.”
Netanyahu did everything he could to bring Otzma Yehudit lawmaker Almog Cohen onto the Likud slate. Cohen himself said there are no longer any differences between Likud and the hard-right Otzma Yehudit. Is Likud no longer the party it once was?
“Likud is a governing party, a responsible party. It is the party of all the people of Israel — of the periphery and the center, Sephardim and Ashkenazim, traditional Jews, secular Jews and Haredim.”
And you aren’t offended when Likud is compared with Otzma Yehudit?
“Likud is not Otzma Yehudit. Likud is the party of the people of Israel.”
Cohen appears to recognize the potential electoral damage posed by legislation that would allow many Haredi, or ultra-Orthodox, men to continue avoiding military service, as well as a measure aimed at preventing the arrest of draft evaders and deserters.
“We need to complete the conscription law,” he said. “We have to increase equality in sharing the burden, and our Haredi brothers must also enlist. Anyone for whom Torah study is not a full-time occupation — 60% of Haredim — must enlist. It is important for security, it is important for the economy and it is important for bringing unity to the people of Israel.”
You could have done that during the last term, and you didn’t.
“The government before us, the Lapid-Liberman government, which was the most anti-Haredi government since the establishment of the state, failed to bring in a single recruit. And we were occupied mainly with managing the war. Unfortunately, there are those who try to diminish the achievements, but the State of Israel’s achievements in this war are unprecedented. All those who challenged the State of Israel did not live to die of old age. Not Hassan Nasrallah, not Yahya Sinwar and not Ali Khamenei. We prevented Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.”
You didn’t prevent it. Maybe you delayed it. Some experts argue that after two rounds against Iran, we are back where we started.
“Fine, we delayed it. But the war against Iran was a tremendous victory and an enormous achievement.”
I’m not sure the public sees it that way. Otherwise, you would be cruising to victory in the election.
“If we hadn’t attacked, Iran would have a nuclear weapon. People in the intelligence community say we delayed Iran’s nuclear program by two, three or four years. One thing is clear: If Iran tries to restart its nuclear program, we will be on our way there to strike. We have already demonstrated our capabilities.”
In other words, Israel needs to strike Iran again?
“I’ll say it again: If Iran makes the mistake of trying to restart its nuclear program or its ballistic missile program, even if there is an agreement with the United States, we will be there to strike.”
There were significant achievements in the campaign against Iran. On the other hand, we achieved none of the war’s three objectives: eliminating the nuclear program, eliminating the ballistic missile program and bringing down the regime.
“If we had not launched that campaign, Iran would already have a nuclear weapon. Look at the State of Israel’s deterrence. The fact is that until a few weeks ago, Iran attacked most of the countries in the region. Who didn’t it attack? The State of Israel, because it knows we have deterrence. To this day, Mojtaba Khamenei has not emerged from the hole where he is hiding. He knows the long arm of the State of Israel can reach anywhere.”
Does Israel have a plan to create a route that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz?
“The prime minister and I are currently working with the United States to advance the creation of a route that would bypass both the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb. The idea is to lay pipeline infrastructure, some of which already exists in Saudi Arabia and Israel.”
What is your biggest achievement at the Energy Ministry and the Foreign Ministry?
“My most significant achievement at the Energy Ministry is that the energy sector functioned flawlessly during the war, despite all those scenarios about blackouts and generators. And, of course, breaking the Israel Electric Corp.’s monopoly is also a very significant achievement. At the Foreign Ministry, after many years, I managed to complete the effort to secure visa-free travel for Israeli citizens traveling to the United States.”
It’s who you know
As someone who came to Likud from former finance minister Moshe Kahlon’s Kulanu party, Cohen has difficulty aligning himself with the confrontational rhetoric directed at the judiciary by Justice Minister Yariv Levin or Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana. Nor is he willing to say he would defy a ruling by the High Court of Justice.
“The government is not above the law, but neither is the court above the law. There is a sense that the balance between the branches of government has been disrupted,” Cohen said. “When we see attempts to interfere with the appointment of Roman Gofman as head of the Mossad or David Zini as head of the Shin Bet, then intervention by the High Court is unnecessary.”
I’m sorry, but the High Court approved both Gofman’s appointment and Zini’s appointment.
“Yes, but I think the petitions regarding Gofman and Zini should have been dismissed outright. They should not even have reached a hearing. We need a court that acts according to the law. We need a court that enjoys the public’s trust. I want a court in Israel that represents all parts of society, like in the United States. The ‘friends appointing friends’ system in the courts has to end. I succeeded in life because of who I am, not because of friends. That is how it should be in the military, in politics and in the judicial system.”
According to media reports this week, Netanyahu is deeply concerned about polling for Likud and the broader right-wing bloc. He reportedly believes he has lost 10 Knesset seats during the current term and is uncertain whether he can win those voters back. Cohen argues that Likud is consistently underestimated in polls.
“In 2015, the polls gave Likud 21 or 22 seats. We finished with 30 seats and won. In the last election, the polls gave our bloc 57 or 58 seats, and we ended up with 64. In other words, there is a bias in the polls. In the actual results, the right always gets stronger. I believe that even those who are undecided and sometimes talk about wanting change, when they come to vote, their hand will tremble. They won’t want a government formed here with the Islamic Movement.”
Maybe their hand won’t tremble because of Oct. 7 and Netanyahu’s responsibility for the deadliest massacre in the country’s history?
“The issue of Oct. 7 needs to be investigated by a national commission of inquiry that examines everyone going back years. But today, the State of Israel is the undisputed power in the Middle East. We have achieved successes on every front. So I’m confident that this time, too, we will get far more than the polls predict.”
There is still a cloud hanging over the issuance of a diplomatic passport to Yair Netanyahu. Why did you get yourself caught up in that affair?
“This investigation should never have been opened because Yair Netanyahu’s passport had been renewed for security reasons several times by several directors-general, beginning in 2009. Diplomatic passports were also issued to mayors, as had been done in the past, because of the international activities they conduct as part of their official duties.”
Your son served in the reserves in Lebanon. You are a member of the Security Cabinet and are expected to make decisions that also concern Lebanon. Does that affect your decision-making?
“I try to make decisions based solely on what is right and best for the security of the State of Israel. Sometimes Security Cabinet decisions mean that my son is also called up for reserve duty. A month ago, he completed several months of reserve service in Lebanon. By day, I’m a Cabinet member, and on quite a few nights, I’m also a worried father. I understand the significance of the decisions we make. And yes, I can tell you that I’m proud of him and his friends.”

articles.title: After giving up on military force, Trump’s new plan to defeat Iran is…more economic sanctions?
articles.body:
On Tuesday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent drew back the curtain on what President Donald Trump called his “Economic D-Day” plan to strangle Iran’s economy instead of using warfare to destroy the state.
It’s very easy to dismiss this plan — which has been, hilariously, dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast” — as another Trump public relations ploy, an effort to convince his dwindling MAGA base that the United States is not suffering a humiliating defeat in the Persian Gulf.
It certainly is that, but there may be even more negative consequences that could arise from this idea, depending on how far the Trump administration wants to push it.
Essentially, the U.S. has threatened anyone — ally and enemy alike — who does not cooperate with their new economic diktats against Iran. The plan won’t work, and Iran is not going to allow the U.S. to decide when the shooting stops. The Islamic Republic will continue to find ways to pressure the U.S. until its demands are met, an outcome the U.S. will eventually be forced to resign itself to.
Trump is giving up on military force
The most glaring implication of this latest stunt is that Trump has been forced to recognize that Iran has defeated the United States militarily. The U.S. has exhausted its military options, and Iran’s government is not only still standing, but it is as strong as it has been in recent memory.
The United States has lost fifteen of its bases in the Gulf region, has catastrophically depleted its reserves of defensive missiles, and has been forced to divert major resources to the region from Asia, essentially abandoning key allies Taiwan, Japan, and South Korea.
The Gulf states, except the United Arab Emirates, have realized that not only is the United States’ commitment to their security unreliable, but even if it does try to fulfill that commitment, its ability to do so is not what they once believed it to be.
Meanwhile, Israel has been exposed as a security liability and a toxic political brand for the United States. Beyond revulsion at Israel’s actions among the American public, it is also now being correctly blamed for getting the U.S. into this self-defeating war, and it is even being exposed, at last, as the real obstacle to ending the genocide in Gaza — refusing to cooperate even with the Board of Peace’s plans, which are wholly favorable to its side.
Iran has certainly suffered in the war, its already reeling economy enduring much greater devastation, and it has borne the brunt of the human cost of the fighting in the Gulf in lives and injuries.
But the Islamic Republic has not only stood firm against American firepower, but the government’s position within the country is also stronger for having withstood two military and nuclear powers. At least for now, opposition in Iran has been muted by a combination of anger at the American-Israeli attack and a strong clampdown on protest.
While Trump and his henchmen will never admit this, they know they’ve lost. More fighting means even more decay of America’s ability to frighten the rest of the world with its unhinged and extremely expensive military prowess.
So they are trying something else. Transferring the lead in the war on Iran from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to Bessent, Trump is trying to present his “Economic D-Day” as something new. But it’s actually more of the same.
It is simply more economic sanctions, a tactic that hasn’t worked for 47 years and isn’t about to work now. Even worse for Trump, Iran is not going to let the U.S. unilaterally decide that the shooting war is over.
Sanctions kill, but sanctions don’t bring change
Bessent offered very few details in his presentation, but it seems clear that the U.S. is going to try to isolate Iran economically by threatening its major trading partners with secondary sanctions if they continue to do business with Iran.
The targets would include both states and financial institutions, but Bessent declined to specify which ones, how deeply the sanctions would hit, or even when they would take effect. He did, however, note that enacting the United States’ plan threatened to “blow up” the global financial system.
The sanctions on Iran have caused inflation to balloon to around 88%, while inflation rates for some food supplies and medicines have climbed as high as 400-600%. The rial’s value has now plummeted past two million to the dollar.
Too often, news reports about such economic warfare are accompanied by people milling about in downtown or market areas. But the reality is that this sort of economic warfare kills and destroys lives.
What it won’t do is force change, at least not without a very specific policy goal. The United States has long used sanctions as a punitive measure. And they do cause plenty of suffering. But they fail as a coercive measure most of the time, largely because the suffering they cause is confined to ordinary citizens rather than rulers, and those citizens respond by rallying around the flag.
The exception that is often pointed to is Barack Obama’s use of sanctions to entice Iran into talks that led to the nuclear deal. But in that case, there was already considerable support in both the government and the populace for the talks, and the sanctions had a specific, clearly communicated goal for Iran. Most of all, the goal was a deal on nuclear weapons, which Iran did not have and was not pursuing.
In most cases, however, sanctions have been used to try to force fundamental change in government, or even to topple those governments. In Cuba, Iraq, Russia, and Iran, for most of the past four decades, among many other places, sanctions were used in an effort to get countries to agree to their own demise — or at least, to conditions that they were never going to see as being in their interests. Under those conditions, there is no example of sanctions being effective.
Global pushback
It is very possible that the United States is, once again, merely blustering and will not actually do much with this plan.
The real difference in this proposal from the decades of sanctions and the “maximum pressure” policy that Trump enacted in his first term (and, it is always worth reminding ourselves, Joe Biden did nothing to reverse) is the emphasis on secondary sanctions.
The idea is that if the U.S. threatens other countries and financial institutions with penalties that might include being completely cut off from the American financial system, they will join in the campaign to isolate Iran’s economy.
The problem is that Iran’s partners have little incentive to bow to American pressure. Iran’s largest trading partner is China, and Beijing has already made it clear they will not give in to U.S. bullying. Indeed, there are laws in China that bar Chinese entities from cooperating with such sanctions regimes. No Chinese firm is more concerned about angering the U.S. than it is about angering its own government.
Other major partners include Iraq, Türkiye, the UAE, Afghanistan, and Pakistan, with trade with the EU being mostly concentrated on Iranian imports. The U.S. could impose sanctions on those countries, but most of them are American allies. And China’s role is not limited to protecting its trade with Iran.
China has its own financial system, centered around the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS). While it is not entirely independent of the U.S. dollar, it has grown since its creation in 2015. The system was created specifically in response to the threat of U.S. sanctions, and while it would not be an ideal situation, it would help cushion the blow for any country that faced U.S. sanctions.
That would also accelerate the global status of the Chinese renminbi and CIPS. It would hasten the demise of the dollar’s primacy as the global currency. At the very least, it would motivate China to accelerate the expansion of its financial system to challenge the U.S.’s dominance of global transactions, and it would be supported by many countries, including many U.S. allies, who don’t want to see the U.S. continue to hold this monopolistic power.
It is highly doubtful that this is something Bessent would want to risk, even if his boss fails to grasp the perils it would pose to the American empire.
That’s why the U.S. is unlikely to pursue the kind of global sanction threat that Bessent was suggesting.
The Iranian response is coming
This threadbare plot is not only an effort to win the war of choice against Iran by other than military means; it is also an attempt by the Trump administration to establish a sense that Washington is controlling the war’s course. That, too, is unlikely to succeed.
The U.S. may not want to continue the shooting war, but Iran has little interest in simply enduring American economic pressure.
Trump’s tactical thinking is much more short-term than Iran’s and is largely focused on the upcoming midterm elections. As Gulf states search for ways to export more oil by routes other than the Strait of Hormuz, Trump believes American voters will see less fighting and lower gas prices. Perhaps not coming down to pre-war levels, but at least, he expects, comfortably under four dollars a gallon.
Iran also understands the importance of the American midterms. It sees growing opposition among Democrats to the war, and a good chance Democrats will win back the House, and possibly the Senate as well.
All of this is part of Iran’s calculations about retaliation. It is not a matter of if, but of when and how that retaliation will come.
Iran has repeatedly shown it will not allow the U.S. to dictate the course of this war. It has also made clear that the demands they articulated in the Memorandum of Understanding earlier this year remain their parameters for ending the war.
Democrats will be even more incentivized to push for any resolution they can get, as they will be able to present perceived losses to Iran as Republican failures ahead of the 2028 election while pocketing the gains from a wide swath of the public for ending the war.
Should Republicans retain control of both houses, or if there is a split, Iran will calibrate its response accordingly. The tenor and intensity of that response will be escalatory in any case. How much will depend on Iran’s tactical needs.
Since it is unlikely “Operation Economic Outcast” will meet with much success, what Iran will probably want to do is to hit American forces and interests hard enough to cause Trump more significant pain politically. They do not want Washington to feel like they can strangle Iran’s economy with impunity.
The U.S. may think the shooting war is over, but Iran does not see it that way, and they are not going to allow the U.S. to dictate a shift to economic warfare, even though that seems like a losing path for Washington as well.

articles.title: ‘Let’s stop being suckers for Ukraine’ – Polish MEP
articles.body:
‘Let’s stop being suckers for Ukraine’ – Polish MEP
Warsaw should stop giving Ukraine free weapons as long as it glorifies Nazi collaborators responsible for massacring Poles, a member of the European Parliament has said.
Earlier this week, Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky again called upon Kiev’s foreign backers to provide more Patriot missiles, citing an acute shortage of air defense munitions amid intensifying Russian strikes on military-related targets across the country.
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski told Ukrainian media on Thursday that Warsaw was ready to cooperate with Kiev on the production of Patriot interceptors for the needs of both NATO and Zelensky’s government.
In a post on X the same day, Zajaczkowska-Hernik expressed her frustration, saying: “More missiles for Patriots for Zelensky for nothing? Let’s stop being suckers for Ukraine!”
Warsaw has provided Kiev with some $4.6 billion in military aid since February 2022, supplying tanks and warplanes, among other things, and “should have pursued a transactional policy” towards Ukraine, she argued.
“We’re handing them valuable equipment and paying off their loans for them, and they spit in our face with the Banderite pantheon of heroes – what the hell is this?!” the MEP wrote.
Relations between Warsaw and Kiev deteriorated in June after Zelensky granted an active Ukrainian commando unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA (Ukrainian Insurgent Army),” prompting outrage in Poland.
The UPA was the armed wing of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), led by Stepan Bandera, which collaborated with Nazi Germany during the early stages of its 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union. UPA fighters massacred up to 100,000 ethnic Polish civilians in 1943-1944 in what is now western Ukraine, according to Polish estimates.
In recent months, the remains of two OUN co-founders – Andrey Melnik and Evgeny Konovalets – were exhumed in Europe and delivered to Ukraine to be reburied as part of a push by Zelensky to build a “Pantheon of outstanding Ukrainians.”
Warsaw warned Kiev that it will not support its bid to join the EU if it does not change its ways, while Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest state honor.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said last week that the neo-Nazi nature of the Ukrainian government had become so visible that even the Polish authorities, who are gripped by Russophobia, cannot help but see it. According to Putin, Warsaw simply cannot ignore the “obvious demand” of its own population to address the issue.

articles.body:
Ukraine has intelligence that Russia is planning new ground offensives against Kyiv and Chernihiv — while Moscow ramps up drone strikes on Ukrainian cities.
Pavlo Palisa, deputy head of Ukraine’s presidential office, told reporters that Russian military chiefs have been tasked by the Kremlin’s political leaders with planning and preparing for attacks on the two cities, according to intelligence received and verified by Ukraine.
Palisa said there is not yet evidence that Russian troops are gathering to carry out the attacks, and that Ukraine’s priority is to “prevent the creation of conditions for the Russians to be able to launch any offensive actions at all.”

articles.title: Warning systems can learn from Nepal
articles.body:
Massive flash floods and landslides struck along the Nepal-China border on Wednesday, killing hundreds and leaving more than 1,000 people missing.
The disaster is noteworthy for Taiwan, as analysts said there was no significant rainfall before it occurred. Initial assessments suggested that a high-altitude rock and ice avalanche blocked a river, forming a barrier lake that suddenly burst.
People have traditionally associated floods with torrential rains, but in an era of increasingly frequent extreme weather and complex disasters, the next deadly flood might not be preceded by heavy rain at all. For Taiwan, which is similarly home to high mountains, steep slopes and short, fast-flowing rivers, this disaster should prompt the nation to re-evaluate its disaster prevention strategies.
Taiwan’s disaster prevention system has improved significantly, but early-warning mechanisms still rely heavily on weather conditions — authorities determine whether it would issue warnings based on factors such as the amount of rainfall and how high water levels have risen. The problem is that disasters causing significant casualties are increasingly likely to involve compound risks. An earthquake could destabilize a mountainside, that landslide could block a river and the resulting upstream waterway could burst without any additional rainfall.
When disasters lack a single, straightforward cause, the government’s meteorological, water resources, geological and forestry agencies might each monitor only one part of the picture, with no single office holding all the pieces of the puzzle.
The next phase of Taiwan’s disaster prevention policy should focus on building a multi-source risk early warning system. The government already has access to satellite imagery, river water levels, rainfall data, earthquake records and slope-displacement data. Artificial intelligence could be used to quickly cross-check this information for anomalies.
For example, if satellite imagery detects a large-scale landslide in a mountainous area while river monitors detect an unusual drop in water levels downstream, that could indicate an upstream blockage. The system could automatically raise the risk level and dispatch drones for confirmation, rather than waiting for rainfall to reach a predetermined threshold before responding. In disaster prevention, one of the most important pieces of lifesaving information is knowing that something is occurring 20 minutes before the disaster strikes.
Early warning systems must also translate into effective evacuation procedures. Once a fast-moving mudslide enters a river valley, it could be too late to escape by the time it becomes visible to the naked eye. The government should establish clearer evacuation protocols for high-risk areas — who issues the alert, where residents should evacuate, how they would be notified at night and who would assist those with impaired mobility should all be determined and rehearsed in advance. Otherwise, no matter how sophisticated the integrated monitoring capability is, if all they send is a message to cellphones, the technology alone cannot save lives.
The disaster in Nepal offers a clear warning: Disaster preparedness must shift from only preparing when we see rain to acting when risks are identified, thoroughly integrating meteorological, water resources, geological and satellite monitoring. The most worthwhile investment is not post-disaster infrastructure, but in that crucial 20 minute window.

articles.title: Ukraine chooses three Western fighters to build its air force around. One of them can fly again from stretch of road in 15 to 20 minutes
articles.body:
Ukraine has decided which Western fighters it will build its air force around. The Air Force settled on three platforms, the Swedish JAS 39 Gripen, the French Rafale, and the American F-16, aviation commander Colonel Oleksandr Diakiv said in a segment by the Air Force Command.
Ukraine entered the full-scale war flying Soviet-era jets and has spent three years assembling a Western fleet. F-16s arrived in 2024 and now fly combat missions. France has delivered Mirage 2000s, and Sweden has pledged to deliver Gripen. The choice narrows Ukraine's field to three types it can sustain, arm, and repair at war tempo.
The choice weighed more than performance
Ukraine assessed every platform that might suit it, Diakiv said, and concluded it could operate three with maximum effectiveness. The decision turned on aircraft and operating costs, weapons, logistics, parts availability, what Ukrainian infrastructure can support, and the speed of repairs and battle-damage recovery.
"We went through all the platforms that were possibly acceptable for us. And we came to the conclusion that Ukraine can use three platforms with maximum effectiveness," Diakiv explained.
The F-16 already operates in Ukraine, so the Air Force has both the aircraft and trained pilots, technicians, and specialists who know its quirks. That experience will speed the adoption of the other Western types, according to Diakiv.
The Gripen suits a country under fire
Also, Diakiv singled out the Gripen, a multirole fighter that can strike air and ground targets and carries Swedish and other European weapons. Its main advantage is that it demands little infrastructure.
The jet can operate from unprepared surfaces and stretches of road and requires minimal ground crew to prepare for another flight in 15 to 20 minutes, according to the commander.
The aircraft is only part of the system
Taking on a new platform is not a matter of handing over jets, Diakiv believes. Weapons, ground support, parts, logistics, and trained people all have to arrive together, and Ukrainian pilots, engineers, and logistics specialists are now training abroad.
"You can buy a plane, you can buy a missile, you can buy a bomb, but you cannot buy experience," Diakiv said.
That combat experience, according to the colonel, is increasingly shaping the aviation coalition, with allies helping Ukraine realize ideas drawn from its own fighting rather than only offering finished solutions.

articles.title: Iraqi factions propose weapons 'freeze' instead of disarmament
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Iraqi factions propose weapons 'freeze' instead of disarmament
Iraqi armed factions have proposed placing their weapons in their own storage facilities and suspending military activity for two years, rather than handing their arsenals to the state, political sources close to the governing Coordination Framework told The New Arab.
The proposal, which Baghdad has rejected, highlights the obstacles facing Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s government as it seeks to bring all weapons under state control without triggering a confrontation with Iran-aligned groups in the country.
Three Iraqi political sources, including a senior parliamentarian, said the government received the proposal in recent days. Under the plan, unnamed factions would halt armed operations and place their weapons in designated warehouses for two years, but would retain control of them rather than transfer them to Iraqi security forces.
A senior Iraqi MP told The New Arab that Kataib Hezbollah was among the groups to have proposed freezing its weapons in private depots and ceasing armed activity inside Iraq for two years.
The group also linked the proposal to the future of US forces in Iraq and demanded assurances that its leaders would not be targeted, the MP said, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter.
"The government rejected the proposal, considering it an attempt to circumvent the principle of ending weapons outside the official security forces," the lawmaker said.
Baghdad is using intermediaries including former Council fo Representatives member Hadi al-Ameri, National Security Adviser Qasim al-Araji and Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) chief Faleh al-Fayyadh to engage with the armed groups, according to the source. No direct meeting has yet taken place between Zaidi and faction leaders or their representatives.
Resistance to disarmament
The most influential factions, with close ties to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, continue to reject surrendering their weapons, while warning they could escalate against the government if it attempts to use force.
Kataib Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba, Kataib al-Wafiyoun and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada have in recent weeks issued public statements setting conditions for any discussion of their weapons.
These include the withdrawal of US and Turkish forces from Iraq, the dismantling of the Kurdistan Region’s Peshmerga forces, an end to what they describe as US influence over Iraq’s political, economic and financial decision-making, and the expulsion of US companies.
Other groups, including Badr, Kataib al-Tufuf and Harakat al-Abdal, have not publicly set out their positions.
Zaidi said last week that his government did not intend to clash militarily with the factions, describing the effort to monopolise weapons in state hands as a "constructive dialogue".
He said some groups had handed over weapons, severed their organisational ties and joined the state-sanctioned PMF, while talks continued with others. Zaidi said political forces broadly supported the effort, which he described as consistent with Iraq’s constitution and necessary to strengthen state authority and stability.
However, sources close to the Coordination Framework said proposals to regulate or freeze the weapons, rather than surrender them, had found little support within the government. They said such arrangements were also unlikely to satisfy Washington or neighbouring states concerned about factions’ drones and missiles, including weapons with a range exceeding 100 kilometres.
Limited visibility over arsenals
A former Iraqi government adviser told The New Arab that Baghdad does not have a reliable database detailing the quantity or types of weapons held by the factions — a gap that makes official claims of progress difficult to assess.
He said the consensus in Baghdad was to avoid a military confrontation, including raids on faction bases and camps, because of the risk of a wider internal conflict and Iran’s influence over the groups.
The Iraqi state has received weapons from several factions, including Harakat al-Imam Ali and Asaib Ahl al-Haq, he said. But the equipment handed over was limited and did not reflect the groups’ full capabilities.
The adviser said Kataib Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada remained the three main factions unwilling even to make a symbolic handover. Together, the groups have around 30,000 fighters affiliated with the PMF, he said, although their organisational structures and armaments remain tied to their respective factions.
Pressure from Washington
Iraqi political researcher Ali al-Taie warned that continued failure to make progress could prompt Washington to withdraw support for Zaidi’s government and revive the use of sanctions against Iraqi state and private-sector bodies.
He argued that Washington would view any formula short of the surrender of drones and missiles as an attempt to evade disarmament. The US, he added, is unlikely to accept transfer of weapons to the PMF as a sufficient solution, viewing many of the factions and the umbrella force as closely intertwined.
Kataib Hezbollah renewed its rejection of disarmament in a statement on 18 August, issuing threats against Zaidi and accusing him of pursuing US-backed policies. The group said that any arrangement with the government required the withdrawal of US forces, the removal of Turkish troops from northern Iraq and the dismantling of the Peshmerga.
Earlier this month, Iraqi MP and parliamentary security committee member Othman al-Shaybani said Zaidi had warned that failure to resolve the weapons issue could invite international — particularly US — intervention.
Shaybani said such intervention could go beyond political pressure and involve strikes on faction sites, a scenario the government is trying to avert through negotiations and efforts to place all armed groups under state authority.

articles.title: China, Russia, Iran leaders to meet
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) are expected tomorrow in Kyrgyzstan for a two-day summit, also attended by Iran’s and India’s leaders, of a regional bloc seeking to be a counter-influence to the West. Around a dozen heads of states would head to the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, to mark 25 years of the Shanghai Cooperation Group (SCO).
The group brings together Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, four Central Asian countries and Moscow-allied Belarus.
Putin and Xi have previously used SCO summits to promote their vision of a multipolar world and present a united front against the West. It takes place four-and-a-half years into Moscow’s Ukraine invasion and six months into the war between Washington and Tehran. Iran would be represented by its president, Masoud Pezeshkian.
Photo: Reuters
Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian as well as Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif are due to take part in a plenary session chaired by Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov.
Putin is expected to hold separate bilateral talks with Pezeshkian and Xi, among other leaders, Kremlin spokesman Yuri Ushakov said.
Russia and Iran — among the most sanctioned states in the world — have massively deepened their military and economic ties during the Ukraine war.
US President Donald Trump has warned Moscow and Beijing against arming Iran. Putin’s meeting with Pezeshkian comes days after the CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a rare trip to Moscow, with US media speculating he could have discussed Ukraine and Iran with his Russian counterparts.
The SCO has historically focused on economic issues. It gained momentum in the past few years under Moscow’s and Beijing’s leadership. On top of its 10 members, it now has 15 “dialogue partners,” including Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. It also has two observer countries: Afghanistan and Mongolia.
The SCO’s founding declaration says the group is “not an alliance directed against other states.”
However, Putin and Xi have repeatedly made anti-Western speeches during its summits.
At last year’s gathering, Putin accused Western countries of provoking the Ukraine war, while Xi denounced “acts of intimidation,” referring to US-Chinese tensions.
The Bishkek summit takes place as some SCO members are amid real wars — the Ukraine and Iran conflicts — or trade wars, with the imposition of US tariffs on Chinese and Indian goods.
This month, the US slapped secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners in the sectors of gold, technology, digital assets, aviation and maritime transport, aiming to cripple the Iranian regime.
Washington also threatened Iran’s allies with sanctions. China, a major importer of Iranian oil, responded by saying it would “firmly defend” its interests.
Iran, living under sanctions since its 1979 revolution ended with Islamic authorities taking charge, has regularly said it will not cave to economic pressure. However, Pezeshkian has acknowledged his country faces “economic difficulties.”
Iran only joined the bloc in 2023. Mohammad Hassan Najmi, an international relations expert, said that Tehran “believes its membership and active participation in these alliances can enable it to circumvent US and European sanctions.”
However, concrete benefits of the group are uncertain, he said, as “in times of crisis, these alliances have rarely allowed Iran to resolve its difficulties.”
While the bloc claims to represent about 40 percent of the world’s population and 25 percent of global GDP, it remains diverse, with some disagreements among members.
Russia and China compete for influence in Central Asia — a resource-rich region crucial for the transport of goods between Europe and Asia — while Beijing at times has had strained relations with India and Pakistan.

articles.title: Taiwan in Time: The once-bustling temple atop 1,200 steps
articles.body:
Aug. 31 to Sept. 6
More than 3 million people visited Taipei’s Zhinan Temple (指南宮) in 1973, making it Taiwan’s second-most visited scenic area that year.
Built in 1891, the temple had been a tourist destination since the Japanese colonial period, when visitors had to initially take a ferry across the Jingmei River before climbing a winding trail up Houshan (猴山).
Photo courtesy of Academia Historica
Its popularity was reflected in popular media. The 1932 tune New Song of the Black Cat and Black Dog (新烏貓烏狗歌) depicted two lovers who prayed at the temple for their marriage. The man couldn’t afford to hire a sedan chair, so they made the arduous journey on foot. They later committed suicide after the man was unable to pay the bride price demanded by the woman’s family.
The 1959 movie Brother Wang and Brother Liu Tour Taiwan (王哥柳哥遊台灣) featured the titular duo huffing and puffing their way up the temple’s stairs on their first stop.
Although visitor numbers have declined from their historic peak, Zhinan Temple remains a destination for many, with the Maokong Gondola making a stop there. Its Lingxiao Hall, completed in 1966, was seriously damaged in a fire on Monday. Officials say the rest of the complex will remain open.
Photo courtesy of National Museum of Taiwan History via Open Museum
DISPUTED ORIGINS
The principal deity of Zhinan Temple is the Taoist immortal Lu Tung-pin (呂洞賓). According to the temple, sacred incense representing Lu Tung-pin’s spiritual presence was brought from China in 1882 by Wang Pin-lin (王斌林), who had been appointed magistrate of Tamsui County. The deity was initially housed in Wanhua District (萬華), but locals later invited it to Jingmei District (景美) during an epidemic. After the sickness passed, local gentry built a small thatched-roof shrine on Muzha District’s (木柵) Houshan in 1890 to honor the deity.
But this account is disputed. The National Taiwan University database of Qing officials lists Wang as a county deputy in Bangka (today’s Wanhua), rather than as Tamsui magistrate. Taiwan Daily News reports suggest that he was already in Taiwan by 1878.
Photo courtesy of Wikimedia Commons
Examining Japanese-era sources, historian Paul Katz traces Zhinan Temple to a spirit-writing temple in Wanhua dedicated to Lu. After hearing of the deity’s powers, Jingmei residents had Wanhua artisans carve an identical statue and established their own temple. Worshippers from nearby Muzha later joined them, and helped establish Zhinan Temple in 1891.
Ethnologist Wu Tsung-ming (吳宗明) argues that Wang was already established on Houshan in the 1880s, where spirit writing may also have taken place. Wang’s son, Wang Yu-ching (王毓卿), later worked with worshippers from Jingmei and Muzha to establish Zhinan Temple and served on its first board.
The temple no longer offers spirit-writing services, having shifted its focus to Taoism, with Buddhist and Confucian characteristics.
At first, visitors had to cross the Jingmei River from Muzha to reach the temple. They could make the crossing on foot when the water was low, writes Hsu Chung-chieh (徐仲杰) in “The formation of the religious attraction of Muzha Zhinan Temple” (宗教景點木柵宮的形成), but taking a ferry was the safer option. Around 1900, as the temple’s popularity grew, Muzha District head Chang Te-ming (張德明) and eight others purchased local farmland and used the collected rent to fund a free ferry service.
A Taiwan Daily News article in 1909 attributed the temple’s popularity not only to the efficacy of its principal deity, but also to the cool mountain air and superb views of Taipei. Lu Tung-pin was said to cure illnesses and provide worshippers with dreams that predict the future.
EXPANDING FACILITIES
Photo courtesy of Lienyuan Lee
The journey to the temple from Muzha’s main street took 30 to 40 minutes, painter Kinichiro Ishikawa wrote in the Taiwan Daily News in 1926, adding that “visiting once was enough.” The “thousand stone steps” leading to the temple already existed by then, and sources show beggars waiting along the route for visitors, Hsu writes.
By the 1920s, visitors could take a train to Jingmei and continue to Muzha by bus or pushcart. The crowds persisted into the intensified Japanization period of the late 1930s, when extra Lunar New Year buses were reportedly required despite government promotion of State Shinto. A 1938 report showed 700,000 to 800,000 visitors per year.
The temple began large-scale renovations and expansion in 1920, a project that took seven years to complete. A temporary wooden bridge was built in 1928 for the opening ceremony, but it survived only a few years before being damaged by torrential rains. The steel Daonan Bridge (道南橋) was completed in 1934, with a ceremony held in October. Although it was conducted by Shinto priests per government policy, it still featured the temple’s deities crossing the river and other Taoist elements.
Visitors continued to use the ferry afterward, although ridership gradually declined.
The stone steps were rebuilt in 1936, with stone lanterns and benches added along the way. Palm and pine trees were planted on either side for shade. Tourist photographers and vendors selling food, drinks and worship supplies set up shop outside the temple.
The temple remained popular after the war. A 1955 report recorded tens of thousands of people visiting during Lunar New Year, prompting bus companies to add more than 100 extra trips to Muzha.
MOTORIZED ERA
Although a road for motorized vehicles was built to the temple in 1955, general Hsu Yung-chang (徐永昌) recalled still hiring a sedan chair to traverse the steps in 1956. The government restricted the number of vehicles during Lunar New Year, and a 1980 United Daily News report described people waiting up to four hours to catch the bus down the mountain.
The grandiose Lingxiao Hall was completed in 1966. The structure was featured in the 1969 Hollywood thriller The Chairman starring Gregory Peck, where it served as a stand-in for Mao Tse-tung’s (毛澤東) residence in Beijing.
That same year, an amusement park and zoo were added to the temple complex, greatly boosting visitor numbers. The park closed in the 1980s, and the temple saw a decline in visitors during the 1990s. Bus routes were reduced, making the remote temple even less accessible.
The idea of building a cable car up to the temple dates back to the Japanese era. A 1932 Taiwan Daily News article briefly pondered the feasibility, and plans were repeatedly floated through the 1950s and 1960s. The gondola finally became a reality in 2007, and the rise of Maokong as a tourist destination brought the temple renewed attention.
Taiwan in Time, a column about Taiwan’s history that is published every Sunday, spotlights important or interesting events around the nation that either have anniversaries this week or are tied to current events.
When we recall the 1990s, we usually identify them as the time of great transitions, from authoritarianism to democracy, and the public’s shift to acknowledging a Taiwanese identity. But another transition occurred, one that we take for granted and hardly notice anymore. The 1980s opened with the massacre of members of the family of democracy activist Lin I-hsiung (林義雄). While Lin was in detention, on Feb. 28, 1980, persons still unknown broke into the Lin family home despite round-the-clock police surveillance. Lin’s mother and two of his three daughters were slain. His eldest daughter survived multiple stab wounds. The following year
During the Martial Law era, newspapers and magazines were strictly controlled by the government. But from 1985 to 1990 — a period that straddled the lifting of martial law in 1987 — a free monthly expat magazine emerged as one of the first published and edited by foreigners. It was also perhaps the first to express a uniquely local expatriate voice. Taiwan Grapevine’s articles were irreverent, politically incorrect and plagued by typos. Neither editors nor writers were named in the magazine, and those bylines that appeared were obvious pseudonyms like Archibald Hellbender. Yet the magazine achieved nationwide distribution. And while
Bloomberg reported earlier this week that the People’s Republic of China (PRC) “has developed hypersonic glide vehicles that can launch air-to-air weapons, an advancement meant to threaten high-value targets such as command-and-control aircraft thousands of miles away.” Military Watch magazine reported in 2024 on one of the designs: “the vehicle is designed with payload options that include electronic warfare and reconnaissance suites, as well as bombs and both supersonic and subsonic drones that detach from the vehicle during flight,” while noting that the PRC is a world leader in such technologies. The threat from the PRC is not only increasing,
Taiwan’s rivers are significantly cleaner today than they were a few decades ago. The country’s rapid industrialization left many waterways polluted by untreated factory discharge, domestic sewage and runoff from livestock operations. Since the 1990s, expansion of municipal sewerage infrastructure and stricter enforcement of environmental standards have turned the situation around. However, freshwater ecosystems now face a very different threat — one that’s far less obvious to people living nearby. “Southern Taiwan — Tainan, Kaohsiung and Pingtung — is facing a particularly critical crisis regarding freshwater biological invasions,” says Lin Yen-ting (林晏廷), an assistant professor in the Master’s Program in Biodiversity

articles.title: After CIA head’s visit to Moscow, Poland’s PM warns Russia is preparing to escalate war. He puts critical window at seven or eight months
articles.body:
Poland's prime minister says the next seven or eight months could decide the region's security. Donald Tusk said there are signs of serious Russian preparations to escalate tensions, both in the war against Ukraine and across the region, according to Ukrinform.
Tusk's warning follows weeks of similar alarms from the countries on NATO's eastern edge. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said on 15 July that intelligence pointed to possible Russian strikes on critical infrastructure in the Baltic states or Poland, according to Defense News.
Poland is the main transit route for Western military aid to Ukraine, which makes its security inseparable from Ukraine's. Tusk himself said in July that Russia could be ready for a confrontation with Europe as early as 2027.
The CIA visit was not the whole of it
At the meeting, reporters asked Tusk about the recent visit of CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow. Poland is in constant contact with the agency's leadership and was not caught off guard by news of Ratcliffe's activity, he said.
Some security information must stay confidential, Tusk added, but that does not mean the public should be deprived of information about the most important threats.
The signals go beyond one trip
The matter is no longer only the CIA director's visit to Moscow, Tusk said. Over recent weeks, numerous public signals have pointed to Russian preparation for escalation.
Russia is very seriously preparing to escalate tensions, both in the war with Ukraine and across the whole region, and that for Russia this fall and winter are meant to be key, he claimed.
Moscow states its aims openly
Some Russian figures have described the war's purpose in plain terms. This week, State Duma vice-speaker Pyotr Tolstoy said Russia views Ukraine as a "territory" that would allow Moscow to export its energy to Europe via a short route, not as a sovereign country.
Tolstoy, whom the EU sanctioned in 2022 as a central figure in Russian state propaganda, also called for massed bombing of Ukrainian cities to break the population into surrender. His remarks are one more public signal of the kind Tusk pointed to.

articles.title: CIA Moscow Trip Warned Against NATO Escalation
articles.body:
Adam Jasser, TVP World’s news director, says John Ratcliffe’s rare Moscow mission appears designed to deter Russian escalation, even as Washington reviews its military footprint in Europe and Belarus raises military readiness.
President Donald Trump may have called CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s Moscow visit “semi-routine,” but it was more likely a warning to the Kremlin against testing NATO’s eastern flank, TVP World news director Adam Jasser said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Jasser told TVP World’s News in Depth program that Ratcliffe’s rare trip was “the central event this week,” arguing that Washington deliberately allowed it to become public as part of its signaling to Moscow.
A warning to Putin
Ratcliffe met Russian foreign intelligence chief Sergei Naryshkin in Moscow on Wednesday. Reuters reported that concerns about possible Russian operations against NATO were raised, although they were not necessarily the main focus.
“I think the simplest explanation is that Mr. Ratcliffe delivered some kind of a warning to Vladimir Putin,” Jasser said.
Trump later said Putin “is not going to be attacking a NATO territory.” Jasser suggested the president may have been expressing confidence that Moscow had understood Washington’s message.
Russia has been expanding military infrastructure capable of supporting up to 115,000 troops near NATO’s Baltic borders.
Kremlin Says Peace Talks on ‘Deep Pause’
Mixed signals from Washington
At the same time, US Under Secretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby was in Brussels discussing the Pentagon’s review of American forces in Europe. The review could reshape the deployment of roughly 80,000 US troops as Washington presses European allies to take greater responsibility for conventional defense.
Jasser said the timing exposed an apparent contradiction: Ratcliffe appeared to be warning Moscow against escalation while Washington was considering reductions in its European military footprint.
“But the main message to Moscow is we have planes in the air. We have troops on the ground still, and we are an alliance,” he said.
Belarus adds another risk. Alexander Lukashenko traveled to Russia after ordering a snap combat-readiness inspection of Belarusian forces. Jasser said Belarus could again serve as a staging ground if Moscow chose to escalate.
“You know, Putin is desperate and desperate. People do silly things, and we can only hope that he doesn’t cross some of these red lines,” Jasser said.

articles.title: Poland, US in advanced talks to relocate Patriot production, says Warsaw
articles.body:
Jo Harper
29 August 2026•Update: 29 August 2026
Warsaw is in advanced talks with the US to relocate some Patriot air-defense system production to Poland, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said Saturday.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said discussions had moved beyond political declarations and were now taking place directly with industry.
A decision is possible in the coming weeks, she said.
“We have gone beyond the stage of political declarations,” Business Insider Polska cited her as saying.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said the talks concern placing part of the Patriot production chain in Poland as demand for the US-made air-defense system rises sharply across Europe.
Poland first formally proposed joint production of Patriot missiles with the US and Ukraine during talks in Washington in July. 
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said at the time that the proposal had been discussed with officials at the Pentagon and State Department.
Earlier this month, she said Poland was already well beyond exploratory talks and that a US decision could come within “a month or two.” 
She also acknowledged that Poland was competing primarily with Germany to secure future Patriot-related production.
The talks come amid growing concern over shortages of Patriot interceptors in Europe and increasing pressure on NATO members to expand domestic production capacity as Ukraine continues to face Russian missile and drone attacks. 
Poland has become one of NATO’s biggest defense spenders since Russia’s war on Ukraine and has placed major orders for US weapons, including Patriot systems, Abrams tanks, HIMARS rocket launchers and F-35 fighter aircraft.
Warsaw has increasingly argued, however, that large-scale arms purchases should also bring technology transfer and production to Poland as it seeks to rebuild its domestic defense industry.

articles.title: Germany preparing ‘extensive’ sanctions on Russia over Leipzig drone plot: Report
articles.body:
Ayhan Simsek
29 August 2026•Update: 29 August 2026
- Germany weighing direct measures against Russian entities
Germany is preparing to formally hold Russia responsible for an attempted explosive drone attack at Leipzig Airport and announce tougher sanctions on Moscow, the weekly newspaper Welt am Sonntag reported on Saturday.
The planned measures would target Russian entities directly and would be coordinated with new European Union sanctions being prepared in Brussels, the newspaper reported, citing German officials familiar with the plans.
An announcement could come in the coming days, possibly around an EU foreign ministers’ meeting in Ireland on Tuesday.
It remains unclear whether Berlin will attribute the attack to individual Russian operatives or to the Russian government itself.
A German government spokesperson declined to provide details, saying any official attribution would follow a review of investigative findings.
According to the report, the measures under consideration go beyond earlier options such as expelling Russian diplomats or closing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
The officials did not specify the tougher steps, but said they could include intensified sanctions or expanded arms deliveries to Ukraine.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz said last week that Germany would impose consequences on those behind the Leipzig incident, without naming Russia.
“The German government will make perpetrators of hybrid attacks pay a price. They will be held accountable,” Merz said, adding that the investigation remains ongoing and that the government would soon present its findings.
Airport attack more serious than initially described
German media reported last week that the attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig Airport earlier this month was more serious than initially described.
The drone had been rigged with explosives, and investigators now believe several drones were involved rather than one, according to public broadcasters NDR and WDR.
Welt am Sonntag also reported that the discovery of a weapons cache near Berlin has hardened the government’s stance.
German domestic intelligence officers found weapons and ammunition in a professionally prepared underground depot in a forest near the capital, authorities confirmed this month.
Federal prosecutors are investigating suspected preparation of a serious violent act threatening the state.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, assesses that the weapons were stashed for Russian spies who could be ordered by Moscow to carry out assassination operations, according to the reports.
The Russian Embassy in Berlin has not issued an official statement on the allegations.
Moscow has previously rejected claims of assassinations, sabotage and spying in countries allied with Ukraine, accusing Western governments of stoking “anti-Russian paranoia.”

articles.title: Zelensky passes buck over civilian deaths after drone depot blast
articles.body:
Zelensky passes buck over civilian deaths after drone depot blast
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky has acknowledged that a drone depot was set up in a residential area outside Kiev after a Russian UAV strike obliterated the facility. Secondary detonations of explosives stored there caused severe damage to the surrounding area, killing at least 27 people in nearby homes.
Later on Saturday, the regional authorities reported that the death toll has climbed to 37.
In a post on his Telegram channel, Zelensky wrote that a warehouse in the village of Milaya had been struck by Russian kamikaze drones, leading to a “subsequent detonation” and “significant destruction of the surrounding infrastructure.” The latter included residential buildings and a nursing home for the elderly, according to the Ukrainian leader.
“Those who allowed this to happen must definitely be held responsible for their decisions,” Zelensky said, adding that the authorities have launched a probe into criminal negligence.
“There cannot be ammunition near houses or other residential buildings,” he concluded.
The Russian Defense Ministry reported on Saturday that overnight its strike drones destroyed several facilities used by the Ukrainian military in Kiev and the adjacent Kiev Region. According to the statement, the depot in the village of Milaya was operated by one of Ukraine’s top arms manufacturers, Fire Point, and contained components of fixed-wing UAVs, which Kiev is using for long-range attacks on Russian territory.
In the wake of the latest disaster in Milaya, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry ordered a nationwide audit of all sites where weapons and munitions are being stored.
This is not the first time Ukrainian civilians have been killed following Russian strikes on such facilities in residential areas.
In early July, an ammunition depot in the city of Vishnyovoe in Kiev Region came under Russian attack, causing huge secondary explosions. As a result, at least seven people lost their lives and around 200 private homes were damaged, with dozens more evacuated.
Back then, Zelensky and other senior Ukrainian officials similarly pledged to end the practice of storing munitions in the middle of residential areas.
Placing military targets in civilian population areas is strictly prohibited under international law and is considered a form of using non-combatants as human shields.

articles.title: FEATURE:Penghu troops prepare for strike
articles.body:
In the pre-dawn darkness on an island in the Taiwan Strait, Taiwanese troops earlier this month pulled long, gleaming 105mm shells from their green plastic canisters. After all the ammunition had been checked and safely loaded through hatches on four tanks, troops waited silently for the order to fire.
The soldiers are among the thousands of troops who form a garrison in Penghu County and they were training for war with China.
A popular tourist destination known for its pristine beaches and coral reefs, the strategically crucial cluster of 90 islands and islets about 50km off the southwest coast of Taiwan proper would be hit in the first wave of an attempted Chinese invasion, senior Taiwanese security officials and military experts said.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
For Taiwan, holding Penghu would allow its forces to resist a Chinese invasion fleet heading toward Taiwan proper, they said.
If Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Navy ships tried to attack Taiwan while bypassing Penghu, they “could be struck by missiles from Penghu,” Institute for National Defense and Security Research research fellow Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲) said.
“That forces the PLA to attack Penghu before it can attack Taiwan,” he said.
By deploying longer-range weapons such as Hsiung Feng III (雄風, “Brave Wind”) missiles on Penghu, Taiwan could also make it harder for the PLA to assemble its forces along the Chinese coast for an invasion, a senior Taiwanese official said on condition of anonymity.
Chinese forces could be targeted even before they set out across the Strait.
If Penghu were taken, the entire Taiwan Strait would effectively fall into China’s hands, they said.
Taipei has been investing in Penghu’s defense, including running programs to beef up the resilience of the 110,000 people who live on the islands in the event of war.
Chinese Ministry of National Defense spokesman Jiang Bin (蔣斌) has said that Taiwan’s plans to fortify the islands were “increasingly absurd and delusional.”
For the troops waiting in the dark during the Aug. 10 drill on the main island of the Penghu group, the quiet was shattered when artillery guns nestled under camouflage netting fired illumination rounds out to sea.
The shells burst with a crump in the distance, casting brilliant light over the ocean approaches.
In a series of maneuvers, the four tanks, along with armored personnel carriers, wheeled forward through clouds of dust, exhaust fumes and explosive gases, blasting away at “invaders” attempting to land.
As sunlight crept across the sea, artillery, mortars and infantry poured fire down over the ocean below. Orange-red tracers from machine guns arched into the sky.
The live-fire drill during the annual Han Kuang exercises was part of rehearsals across Taiwan to resist landings by air and sea.
In the same week, the navy’s Coastal Operations Command were deployed to Penghu for the first time, sending Hsiung Feng missile launch vehicles to beachfront positions in anti-ship and anti-landing operations, military officials said.
Penghu’s strategic location, along with the presence of such weapons, makes the islands a prime target for the PLA, Su said.
Taiwan’s two other major outlying counties, Kinmen and Lienchiang, are too close to China to be a useful part of a defensive network, he said.
However, Taiwanese forces could catch invading Chinese ships in a crossfire of missiles between the Penghu islands and Taiwan proper, Su said.
Missiles on the islands could also launch “counterstrikes” further into China’s hinterland, he added.
The defense ministry is pushing the use of uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAV) to defend Penghu.
The military established the first drone force on the islands last month and UAVs were deployed during the Han Kuang exercises.
Beijing tightly restricts public discussion of military plans related to Taiwan, although Chinese strategists have previously identified the importance of Penghu.
Retired Chinese lieutenant general Wang Hongguang (王洪光) in 2019 suggested that the PLA “strategically suppress” Taiwan by occupying the Penghu Islands.
During a war game attended by retired Taiwanese, US and Japanese military officials last year, Penghu fell just a day after China began surprise long-range attacks on military and infrastructure targets across Taiwan.
The quick capitulation to the PLA startled Taiwanese participants, a report of the activity said.
Asked about that war game, the ministry referred to Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo’s (顧立雄) statement last year that the government takes such exercises into account when making adjustments to its defensive plans.
While the Taiwanese military trains to repel a Chinese landing, Penghu officials and residents are preparing to play their part.
Yen Min-ching is one of about 1,200 people on Penghu who have been certified by the government’s Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience Program. Volunteers are trained to provide support, including first aid, in the event of emergencies such as earthquakes and invasions.
Yen, a retired police officer who is a neighborhood warden, is acutely aware of Penghu’s exposed position between the Chinese coast and Taiwan proper, and has encouraged residents to sign up for the program.
By the end of the year, about 200,000 Taiwanese are expected to have completed the training.
“We absolutely need to have a sense of crisis,” said Husi (湖西) Township Mayor Chen Chen-chung (陳振中), whose district hosts key infrastructure, including cargo transport docks, an airport used for civil and military purposes, and Penghu’s main power plant.
Penghu County “would definitely be one of the first places attacked,” said Chen, who leads about 100 people in a civil defense group that is tasked with wartime support missions.
Those might include distributing rations, setting up defensive fortifications and countering enemy propaganda.
Local businesspeople such as auto workshop owner Ho Chi-hua have signed agreements to cooperate with Taiwanese authorities.
During a drill this month that simulated a scenario in which military logistics facilities were damaged, rifle-carrying troops joined Ho’s staff as they practiced emergency repairs on military vehicles.
Penghu is also preparing for Chinese coercion that stops short of a military attack: Beijing could impose a blockade on Taiwan, which could quickly choke Taipei’s trade-dependent economy and leave outlying islands isolated.
Locals starved of supplies might quickly capitulate, said Kao Yu-jou, a 15-year-old student in Penghu. “People might think: Let’s surrender first, get something to eat, and after I’m full, then we’ll see.”
However, taxi driver William Chen said he would resist.
“If my homeland were invaded, there’s no way I could just stand by,” he said.
Magong (馬公), Penghu’s urban center, has rehearsed its response, holding drills that simulate a blockade and all-out combat, Mayor Huang Jian-zhong (黃健忠) said.
Municipal authorities have signed agreements with grocery stores, pharmacies and construction companies to safeguard emergency supplies and repair capabilities if a crisis occurs, government documents show.
The islands have been a springboard for invasions of Taiwan over the centuries. When Taiwan was a Japanese colony during World War II, the harbor was the target of Allied bombing attacks late in the conflict.
Some analysts think Penghu would provide stiff resistance.
The prospect of heavy losses during WWII had prompted US war planners to cancel a planned offensive on the islands as part of a wider invasion of Taiwan, US Naval War College associate professor Ian Easton said.
“My guess is that if the terrible crunch ever comes, the PLA will find these islands a tough nut to crack,” he said.
